sec.title: Background
sec.p: Emerging evidence indicates that elevated systemic iron levels and dysregulated iron metabolism are closely associated with the pathogenesis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Observational studies have linked iron overload (e.g., hereditary hemochromatosis) to an increased risk of HCC, potentially mediated through iron-induced oxidative stress, DNA damage, and chronic inflammatory responses. However, the causal relationship between specific iron-related factors—such as organ-specific iron accumulation, systemic iron metabolism disorders, or exogenous iron exposure (dietary/drug iron)—and HCC development remains unconfirmed.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: The data of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) involving a variety of human iron content indicators were collected and summarized, covering multiple dimensions such as liver iron content, spleen iron content, pancreas iron content, dietary iron content, drug iron content, and serum iron content, and the information related to genetic diseases of iron metabolism was also included. To explore the potential causal association between iron metabolism disorders and the risk of HCC using two-sample univariate and multivariate Mendelian randomization (MR) techniques. The inverse variance weighting (IVW) method was used as the main analysis method.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: No significant level of pleiotropy was detected according to the MR pleiotropy residual test. Cochran’s Q test and MR-Egger regression analysis did not find evidence of heterogeneity and directional pleiotropy of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). The results of univariate MR Estimation based on the IVW. method show that Liver iron content (OR = 1.0009, CI = 1.0005–1.0013, p = 9.6499e-06) and disorders of iron metabolism (OR = 1.0000, CI = 1.0000-1.0001, P = 4.0417e-08) were the causes of liver cancer. There was no evidence of a causal relationship between drug iron(OR = 1.0176, CI = 0.9612–1.0773, p = 0.5486), dietary iron(OR = 0.9843, CI = 0.9683–1.0007, p = 0.0603) and HCC. Multivariate MR Estimation results based on the IVW method showed that no significant causal association was found between liver iron content, spleen iron content, pancreas iron content, serum iron content, iron metabolism disorder, and HCC risk after using the IVW method.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The univariate results may reflect the complexity of the true association, which needs to be further explored in combination with other methods.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a common malignant tumor of the liver, which seriously threatens human health. Early-stage clinical manifestations are typically insidious and nonspecific, easily overlooked, particularly in patients with chronic liver diseases (e.g., cirrhosis, viral hepatitis), where symptoms may be masked by the underlying liver conditions [1]. HCC is closely related to chronic liver diseases such as hepatitis C, hepatitis B, and cirrhosis. These chronic liver diseases not only create conditions for the growth of HCC but also “fuel the wave” in its development, with poor effective treatment, making the prevention and treatment of HCC a challenging task in the medical field [2]. In the past decades, although the medical field has made significant progress in diagnostic technology and treatment strategies, Hepatocellular carcinoma, is a common and extremely challenging malignant tumor, its overall prognosis is still extremely worrying and not at all optimistic [3]. Its high morbidity and mortality continue to encourage researchers and clinicians around the world to explore its pathogenesis, diagnostic methods, and innovative treatment models, aiming to improve the quality of life and the survival rate [4, 5].

Iron is mainly stored in hemoglobin, and excess iron is stored in the liver parenchyma as ferritin. Iron plays a crucial role in the human body as a cofactor for various proteins and enzymes, which can provide energy for cells, promote cell proliferation, and repair damaged tissues [6]. When the content of iron exceeds the normal range of the human body, it will encourage the excess iron to undergo a Fenton reaction, producing excessive reactive oxygen species(ROS) and other peroxides(Lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH), protein peroxides, and nucleic acid peroxides) to damage cells [7]. It has been shown that cancer cells require the involvement of iron during the stages of tumor development, survival, dissemination, and metastasis [8]. Furthermore, it has been observed that cancer cells exhibit enhanced iron uptake and retention. This phenomenon implies that cancer development is reliant on iron. For instance, certain proteins related to iron metabolism, such as the transferrin receptor, ferritin, and divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1), display upregulated expression in cancer cells. This upregulation drives an increase in the iron content within cancer cells, potentially fueling their growth and proliferation [9, 10].

Mendelian randomization (MR) is a highly innovative approach that uses single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) as a genetic tool to explore the causal relationship between exposure factors and study outcomes. SNPS are genetically stable and have a relatively fixed distribution frequency in the population. With these characteristics, the MR Method allows SNPS to play a key role in penetrating the disease surface and accurately measuring the effect of exposure factors on the process of disease [11]. This approach has the power to minimize confounding and is therefore independent of self-selected lifestyle and environmental factors. Furthermore, it overcomes reverse causality because gene randomization predates disease development [12]. We used MR To assess possible causal relationships between human iron levels, drug iron intake, dietary iron intake, and disturbances in iron metabolism with HCC.

sec.title: Data sources
sec.p: This study investigates the causal relationship between iron metabolism-related biomarkers and HCC using a MR framework. This framework leverages genetic variants (single nucleotide polymorphisms, SNPs) as instrumental variables to infer causality while minimizing confounding and reverse causation. Specifically, we employed a two-sample MR design using summary-level genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from independent European-ancestry cohorts. The exposure factors include: liver iron content (GWAS ID: ebi-a-GCST90016674), serum iron levels (ukb-b-20447), pancreas iron content (ebi-a-GCST90016676), spleen iron concentration (ebi-a-GCST90101831), drug iron (ukb-b-18395), disorders of iron metabolism (finn-b-E4_IRON_MET), and dietary iron intake (ukb-b-14863). The outcome data were derived from the HCC genome-wide association study (GWAS ID: IEU-B-4953) in the IEU OpenGWAS platform (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/), comprising 372,184 European-ancestry individuals and 6,304,034 SNPs (Table 1). To mitigate confounding bias from population stratification, the analysis was strictly restricted to European-ancestry populations. As this study utilized anonymized summary-level data from public databases, it was exempt from ethical review in accordance with Article 32 of the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Selection of genetic instruments
sec.p: The selection of genetic instruments followed a standardized three-stage analytical framework to ensure methodological rigor: (1) Initial screening employed a genome-wide significance threshold of P < 5 × 10− 6(relaxed from the conventional 5 × 10− 8 threshold to enhance statistical power) with stringent linkage disequilibrium (LD) control (r²< 0.001 and physical distance > 10,000 kb) using PLINK’s clump algorithm; (2) MR assumption validation systematically verified: (i) relevance assumption through SNP-exposure association strength (F-statistic > 10), (ii) independence assumption by excluding SNPs associated with HCC confounders (e.g., alcohol intake, viral hepatitis) via PhenoScanner v2 (P < 1 × 10− 5) [13], and (iii) exclusion restriction assumption using MR-Egger intercept tests and Mendelian Randomisation Pleiotropy RESidual Sum and Outlier (MR-PRESSO) global tests to detect horizontal pleiotropy (SNPs with pleiotropy P < 0.05 were excluded); (3) Sensitivity analyses further evaluated robustness through multivariable MR to disentangle independent causal effects of exposures and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses to identify SNPs disproportionately driving causal estimates. Univariate MR was used to assess the causal relationship between each pair of exposures and outcomes [14]. For the important risk factors identified by the univariate MR analysis, multivariate MR analysis was further performed to accurately determine whether these causal risk factors are independent of each other (Fig. 1).

caption.p: Workflow for Mendelian Randomization (MR) analysis of iron-related exposures

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Univariate and multivariate MR analyses were performed in this study using the TwoSampleMR package in R 4.4.2 software. In the univariate MR Analysis, we used the IVW method, weighted median (WM), and MR-Egger method to estimate the effect of exposure factors on the outcome [15]. However, for multivariate MR Analysis, we used the regression-based IVW method. Here, IVW is essentially a means of weighting the mean of random variables. Specifically, the weight assigned to each random variable is the inverse of its variance. In the whole research process, the IVW method was used as the core statistical analysis method, supplemented by the MR-Egger method and WM method to form an effective supplement to the IVW method to ensure the completeness and reliability of the analysis results. To strictly control the problem of horizontal pleiotropy, we introduced the outlier global test (MRPRESSO) and MR pleiotropy residual method to test it. Outliers (i.e., SNPs with a P value of less than 0.05) were eliminated once horizontal pleiotropy was detected IVW method was used to measure the variation among SNPs. For the heterogeneity test, Cochrance’s Q statistic was used. In the key subject analysis phase, if no heterozygosity was detected, the fixed effect IVW method would be used, and if heterozygosity was detected, the random effect IVW method would be used. In addition, to further verify the robustness of the results, we also used MR-Egger regression, weighted median, weighted mode, and other methods to carry out a series of sensitivity analyses to ensure the scientific validity and credibility of the research conclusions [16].

sec.title: Univariable MR analysis of risk factors on HCC
sec.p: A clear causal association between liver iron content and disturbed iron metabolism and HCC was demonstrated in univariate MR analysis in a European population (, 2). Liver iron: OR = 1.0009 (95% CI 1.0005–1.0013, p = 9.6499e–6), indicating that the risk of HCC increased by about 0.09% for every 1 unit increase in liver iron. Disorders of iron metabolism: OR = 1.0000(95% CI 1.0000–1.0001, p = 4.0417e–08), indicating that the cumulative effect of disorders of iron metabolism on HCC was more significant. The possible mechanism is that the dysregulation of regulatory proteins such as hepcidin leads to the imbalance of systemic iron homeostasis, exacerbates oxidative stress and chronic inflammation in the liver, and forms a cancer-promoting microenvironment. The current evidence does not support significant causal relationships between other iron-related biomarkers - serum iron (OR = 0.9998, 95% CI: 0.9984–1.0012, p = 0.8241), splenic iron (OR = 0.9996, 95% CI: 0.9985–1.0008, p = 0.5411), and pancreatic iron (OR = 0.9998, 95% CI: 0.9991–1.0006, p = 0.6766)-and HCC risk. Similarly, exogenous iron supplementation pathways, including pharmacological iron (OR = 1.0176, 95% CI 0.9612–1.0773, p = 0.5486) and dietary iron (OR = 0.9843, 95% CI 0.9683–1.0007, p = 0.0603), showed no statistically significant causal associations with HCC development (all p > 0.05) (Fig. 2).

sec.title: Multivariable MR analysis of risk factors on HCC
sec.p: Ten genetic variants were included for multivariate MR analysis. The heterogeneity test showed that there was a certain degree of heterogeneity among SNP sites (Q statistic = 10.346, P = 0.066), suggesting that the original estimates may be affected by pleiotropy bias, resulting in reduced validity of the instrumental variables. However, no evidence of directional pleiotropy was found in the MR-Egger regression analysis (regression intercept = 9.956 × 10− 5, P = 0.7413), indicating that the association between genetic variants and outcomes was mainly mediated by exposure rather than other pathways. The multivariable MR analysis demonstrated no significant causal association between liver iron content (OR = 1.0001, 95% CI 0.9983–1.0019, P = 0.9057) or iron metabolism disorders (OR = 1.0000, 95% CI 0.9999–1.0002, P = 0.3876) and HCC. Furthermore, the IVW method revealed no significant causal relationships of splenic iron content (OR = 0.9996, 95% CI 0.9982–1.0010, P = 0.5343), pancreatic iron content (OR = 1.0004, 95% CI 0.9969–1.0038, P = 0.8406), or serum iron levels (OR = 1.0047, 95% CI 0.9936–1.0158, P = 0.4095) with HCC risk (Table 3). The current evidence does not support the causal effects of iron metabolism-related biomarkers (hepatic, splenic, pancreatic, and serum iron levels) on HCC risk.

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: We used the tool for MR estimation with the MR-Egger method to examine the heterogeneity of HCC. However, no statistically significant results were found (intercept: – 5.5256e–05 (Liver iron content), 0.0002(Spleen iron content), – 4.9210e–05 (Pancreas iron content), – 7.9059e–05(Serum iron), – 1.7358e–05(Disorders of iron metabolism), – 0.0002(Drug iron), and 0.0002(Dietary iron)). We applied Cochran’s Q statistic using the IVW method to assess homogeneity. The results showed no significant differences (Liver iron content: Q = 12.1545; Spleen iron content: Q = 17.6709; Pancreas iron content: Q = 14.3962; Serum iron: Q = 4.6100; Disorders of iron metabolism: Q = 10.0187; Drug iron: Q = 17.2431; Dietary iron: Q = 17.1281; all P > 0.05)(Table 4). In the leave-one-out analysis, the MR analysis did not change significantly due to any single SNP, and the direction of the causal relationship estimate did not alter either Fig. 3.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: At present, the main treatment methods for HCC are liver resection, liver transplantation, transcatheter arterial chemoembolization, local ablation therapy, etc [17]. In recent years, targeted therapy has gradually become popular. However, due to the insidious onset of HCC, once diagnosed, it is in the middle and advanced stage, and the current treatment methods still cannot improve the survival rate of patients with HCC [18]. Liver cancer is still one of the diseases that threaten human health worldwide and increase the medical and economic burden of countries. Iron is an essential trace element in the human body. When the body’s iron content exceeds the safe limit, it leads to the denaturation of ferritin, which stores iron, and iron ions are released into the cytoplasm of hepatocytes [19]. Excessive iron deposition induces hepatic injury, with growing evidence supporting iron overload as an independent risk factor for primary liver cancer [20, 21]. Emerging evidence further implicates hepatic iron overload as a cofactor in hepatocarcinogenesis, particularly in the context of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), where iron synergizes with lipotoxicity to amplify oxidative DNA damage [22].

In this study, we applied the MR approach to in-depth analysis of pooled genetic data from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to assess the potential causal association between human iron levels and the risk of HCC. The results reveal a significant causal relationship between liver iron content and the occurrence of HCC. On the one hand, the excessive accumulation of iron in hepatocytes can strongly drive oxidative stress response, break the redox homeostasis in cells, and put cells in a state of stress damage. On the other hand, iron accumulation also induces abnormal activation of the cell death program and forced disturbance of liver regeneration. These synergistic effects cause DNA damage in cells to accumulate layer by layer like a “snowball”, which eventually lays the “curse” for the malignant transformation of hepatocytes and promotes the occurrence and development of HCC.

Under normal circumstances, the body can precisely regulate the amount of iron in the whole body through the absorption, storage, and recycling of iron to achieve balance. From the perspective of iron balance regulation, abnormal iron metabolism can be regarded as a decompensated state caused by iron imbalance in the body, which can be caused by environmental factors, genetic factors, and dietary factors or secondary to some diseases. Iron deficiency results in decreased production of hemoglobin in the body, leading to anemia; Iron overload and excessive deposition may cause the body to produce a large number of free radicals and damage organs and tissues. These findings suggest that the regulation mechanism of iron metabolism is closely related to abnormal iron metabolism, which can seriously harm the health of the body. Excess iron in the body is mainly stored in hepatocytes, and increasing evidence has shown that liver iron overload is a risk factor for primary liver cancer. Studies have shown that the hepatotoxicity and hepatocarcinogenesis of iron are based on a large number of ROS produced by the Fenton reaction, which cause DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, and protein denaturation, leading to hepatocyte necrosis and apoptosis. Studies have shown that the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling pathway plays an important role in tumor metastasis, and iron can regulate hypoxia to control the expression of HIF α in the central nervous system [23]. Elmonem et al. found that hepcidin mRNA expression was decreased in chronic hepatitis C compared with normal tissues, and even lower in HCC tissues, suggesting that hepcidin expression is iron content dependent in the progression of liver cancer [24]. Tan et al. reported that the expression of transferrin, a target of hepcidin, was increased in liver cancer tissues [25]. Tian et al. found through their study that there may be no causal relationship between iron status (Ferritin, Transferrin saturation, and Transferrin) and the risk of primary liver cancer [26]. Our MR findings align with the downregulation of hepcidin in HCC progression, suggesting that impaired iron sequestration may drive carcinogenesis. Our study provides novel insights into the causal relationship between iron metabolism and HCC through MR analysis. However, several limitations must be acknowledged, and future research directions should address these gaps to strengthen the validity and generalizability of our findings. While our study focused on European populations to minimize confounding from genetic heterogeneity, this design limits the extrapolation of results to other ethnic groups [27]. Emerging evidence highlights significant interethnic differences in iron metabolism and HCC risk profiles [28, 29]. Future studies should prioritize multi-ethnic cohorts to evaluate whether the observed causal relationships hold across diverse populations. Additionally, stratified analyses by age, sex, and comorbidities (e.g., viral hepatitis or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) are critical [30]. Recent work by Abboud et al. has elucidated sex-specific influences on HCC pathogenesis and clinical outcomes, underscoring the imperative for sex-stratified analytical approaches in hepatocarcinogenesis research [31]. The inconsistency between univariate and multivariate MR findings may stem from unmeasured confounding or insufficient statistical power [32]. Expanding sample sizes through collaborative consortia (e.g., the HCC Genomics Consortium) would bolster statistical precision. Furthermore, integrating omics data (e.g., proteomics or metabolomics) could elucidate mediating pathways. Our findings align with recent preclinical studies highlighting the role of hepatic iron deposition in promoting oxidative stress and genomic instability [33]. However, the lack of association between serum iron and HCC contrasts with epidemiological reports [34]. This discrepancy may reflect tissue-specific iron effects, as demonstrated by Nanba et al. who found that Low baseline levels of the intracellular iron regulators of FBXL5 in addition to a suppressed hepcidin level might be associated with severe hepatic iron deposition in HCC patients [35]. Future MR studies should incorporate tissue-specific iron biomarkers (e.g., MRI-derived liver iron quantification) to validate these mechanisms.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This MR study systematically evaluated the causal relationships between iron metabolism-related biomarkers and HCC, revealing that elevated liver iron content (OR = 1.0009, p = 9.6499 × 10⁻⁶) and disorders of iron metabolism (OR = 1.0000, p = 4.0417 × 10⁻⁸) were significantly associated with HCC risk in univariable analyses, suggesting hepatic iron overload and systemic iron dysregulation may drive hepatocarcinogenesis via oxidative stress and DNA damage. However, these associations became non-significant in multivariable MR (liver iron: p = 0.9057; iron metabolism disorders: p = 0.3876), potentially reflecting confounding or complex interactions among variables. Exogenous iron exposure (pharmacological or dietary) showed no causal links to HCC (p > 0.05), underscoring endogenous iron dysregulation as a key pathological mechanism. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness, with no significant heterogeneity (Cochran’s Q p > 0.05) or horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept p > 0.05). As the first MR study to validate hepatic iron accumulation as a causal risk factor for HCC, this work provides genetic evidence supporting iron overload in carcinogenesis; however, limitations include European ancestry-restricted samples, lack of tissue-specific iron biomarkers, and inconsistencies between univariable and multivariable results. Future research should validate findings in multi-ethnic cohorts using advanced imaging (e.g., MRI-based liver iron quantification), integrate proteomic/metabolomic data to elucidate mechanistic pathways, and conduct sex- and age-stratified analyses to explore population heterogeneity. Collectively, these findings highlight the role of endogenous iron metabolism disruption in HCC development, offering a theoretical basis for clinical interventions such as iron chelation therapy, though further studies are needed to clarify biological mechanisms and translational implications.

notes.title: Ethics approval and consent to partcipate
notes.p: This human study did not require ethical review and approval, as it was conducted using summary data derived from a publicly accessible database. The data used in this study were anonymized and de-identified, ensuring that no individual participants could be identified. All analyses were performed in compliance with relevant guidelines and regulations for research involving publicly available data.
